analysis.title: End of Week Market Intelligence: as goes...
key_insights: US stocks were trading lower Friday 10/16 and on pace for a 1.5%+ weekly loss for the S&P 500 (as of 1:00PM). Drivers were stress in credit markets and the AI trade, higher than expected September core inflation, against a backdrop of $105+/bbl oil, 10%+ import tariffs, an ongoing Middle East war and 10-year Treasury yields above 5%.

GS frames a chain of dependencies: as oil goes, so go rates (higher oil lifts inflation and rates). As rates go, so goes AI (higher rates squeeze the economics of new data centers and slow the AI infrastructure build-out). As AI goes, so goes growth (the US economy depends on the AI build-out to offset an affordability crisis and a moribund housing industry).

Amanda Lynam's note 'AI, Credit, and a Higher Cost of Capital' says higher rates have raised questions about funding for AI capex, leading to a correction across some risk assets, particularly USD high yield credit.

GS forecasts USD IG and HY project finance issuance to grow to $300bn in 2027 from $37bn a year ago, in addition to $420bn of direct hyperscaler issuance forecast for next year. Lynam ring-fences the issue because the US corporate credit market is large enough to absorb it: over $2 trillion of IG debt alone is estimated to be issued in 2026, and $1.5 trillion had been absorbed through July.
September core CPI rose 0.33% and core PPI also came in above expectations. GS economists raised their September core PCE forecast by 14bp to 0.34%.

Fed Chair Warsh signaled that a rate hike at the late-October FOMC meeting is getting less likely, describing the world as having 'broadly conformed to our expectations'. GS says this lowers the odds of a policy error (hiking into a growth slowdown).

The 10-year Treasury yield rose 13bp to 5.32% on the hot CPI, then fell 25bp over the next 24 hours to about 5.13% on Friday afternoon, still about 5bp below the pre-CPI level. GS says the bond market quickly set the inflation data aside and focused on the growth trajectory.
GS economists raised their 3Q26 GDP tracking estimate by 20bp to 3.3% after a stronger than expected industrial production report and signs of more business inventory building.

Week ahead: earnings season continues with a large group of 3Q reports across industries. The macro calendar is light, with housing sentiment and starts and the University of Michigan consumer sentiment survey.

tension_points.bull_case: The US economy remains surprisingly resilient: GS raised its 3Q26 GDP tracking estimate to 3.3%, the Fed signaled a late-October hike is less likely, and the large corporate credit market can absorb heavy AI-related issuance.
tension_points.bear_case: Higher oil lifts inflation and rates, which squeezes data center economics and slows the AI build-out the economy depends on. Credit markets, especially USD HY, already corrected on funding questions.
